newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: OLYMPICS-NEW DRUG TESTING DEVELOPED FOR 2000 OLYMPICS.
newsitem.headline: OLYMPICS-NEW DRUG TESTING DEVELOPED FOR 2000 OLYMPICS.

text.p: The world's top anti-doping experts fired a warning shot at drug cheats on Wednesday, saying they will have developed ways of detecting previously undetectable drugs in time for the 2000 Olympics.
The announcement came after two days of meetings featuring 31 of the world's top sport medicine experts.

They had gathered at the International Olympic Committee (IOC) headquarters to share research into ways of combating the use of human growth hormone, testosterone and EPO (erythropoietin), the stealth drugs of sport.
The substances have become increasingly popular with athletes because all three appear naturally in the body and are extremely difficult to detect.
"At the end of these two days there is a lot to be positive about," said Prince Alexandre de Merode, chairman of the IOC medical commission.
The war against factory produced testosterone will be waged by a newly-developed, highly-sensitive, isotop ratio mass spectrometer.
"This will be the gold medal standard for detecting testosterone and any other steroids," said American Cedric Shackelton, adding that the procedure was ready for implementation.
"Simply put, the new spectrometer is able to distinguish between factory-produced testosterone and the testosterone made in the body."
A substance proving harder to detect is human growth hormone (HGH).
So difficult in fact, that there is very little research into how widespread the use of HGH is.

"We just don't know in which sports or how prevalent human growth hormone use is," admitted Peter Sonksen, director GH 2000, an IOC-backed research project into HGH. "All our information is word of mouth or contraband recovered by drug agencies."
What is known is that HGH is the ideal substitute for steroids. It is found in the body and, like steroids, allows the athlete to build muscle and work harder with a shorter recovery time.
"We want to develop a methodology that will allow us to detect human growth hormone abuse in a reliable fashion in time for the 1999 World Games and then Sydney 2000," said Sonksen.
Testing for EPO, which enhances performance by increasing the number of oxygen-carrying red blood cells, is already carried out by some sports, including cycling and cross-country skiing.
